comments.text: The W.A.C. Bennett Dam (Williston Lake) holds roughly 74 cubic kilometres of water, making it the largest reservoir in British Columbia by volume. There used to be a visitor center at Mica.  Just last week I stumbled across photos of myself there in my early teens (circa 1994)  One shot is me standing on top of the turbine casing right next to the spinning shaft.

I also remember walking through the tunnels carved in the rock, the empty rock cavern for Units 5&6, and the huge pipes containing SF6 to insulate the HV bus.

I've also had the good fortune to be able to visit Revelstoke during a real open house and walk the floor of the generator hall (not the Disneyfied experience you normally get)

replies.author: @martindavis9826
replies.text: That was originally written to sound the alarm over the full implications of building the Mica Dam. Under threats by lawyers, he changed it to a novel and published it. I havent read it but doesnt it end with the Hanford nuclear facility and radioactive waste storage site getting swept out into the Pacific? Worst case scenario is if a large earthquake breaches the Mica Dam, causing the other dams to fail like dominoes as the overall volume keeps increasing with the release of multiple resovoirs. The valley itself is a fault line that runs under all the dams. Mica is just downriver of the Rocky Mountain Trench, another major fault. Also, waves from rockslides into water have caused tsunamis up to 524 metres high (Alaska, 1958). The large capacity of the Arrow Lakes could probably prevent the worst case scenario, along with emergency releases from downstream resovoirs in anticipation of the coming surge. Seasonal high volumes could make it worse. So, who knows? Engineers are often wrong.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: I found it! Christopher Hyde's The Wave, originally published in 1979. And it's actually about Mica Dam failing and triggering a disaster down the Columbia River!
